description: Space11 is a student team that combines curiosity about space with a passion for exploring and creating. Through the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to use open data to develop creative solutions to real-world problems on Earth and in space. Our team brings together students interested in research, storytelling, design, and technology.
summary:
Mars is not a graveyard of cold metal it is humanity's proudest open-air museum, where silent pioneers wait on a dusty red porch for us to catch up.

We developed "The Happiest Retirees of Mars," a Pixar-style 3D animated short film where Ingenuity, Opportunity, Viking 1, and InSight tell their own stories.

Addressing the "Abandoned But Not Forgotten" challenge, our film flips the narrative of discarded hardware: chipped rotors and drained batteries become badges of honor. Through first-person storytelling, real NASA telemetry 72 flights in razor-thin air, 15 years on a 90-day ticket, and 1,300 Marsquakes transforms cold engineering into living memory.

Why does it matter? Because data informs the mind, but metaphor moves the heart. When children see inactive rovers not as broken junk, but as elders holding a relay baton in the Martian dust, a dead battery stops being a period and becomes a comma waiting for the next generation of explorers to write the next line.
details:
“Mars’s Happiest Retirees” is a 4-minute-20-second, Pixar-style 3D animated educational short film created for the “Abandoned but Not Forgotten” challenge. Our project doesn’t present retired Mars spacecraft as lifeless technical data. Instead, it invites viewers to look through an observatory telescope and discover a cheerful retirees’ club on the Red Planet. Ingenuity, better known as Ginny, guides viewers in her own words. Along the way, they meet Opportunity, Viking 1 and InSight, each of whom turns real NASA telemetry into a warm and memorable story. The film reframes this silent equipment as proud pioneers resting in an open-air museum. This helps students, teachers and young dreamers form an emotional bond with space exploration and planetary heritage. The film also turns STEM concepts such as atmospheric density, coaxial rotor physics, hematite evidence for water and Martian seismology into an accessible classroom resource. That resource inspires the next generation of engineers to carry the torch of exploration.

We held to three core principles during production. The first was chronological and scientific visual continuity, so we tracked mission timelines carefully. Ginny’s carbon-fiber rotor blades appear intact in the scenes set in 2021. The broken blade tip appears only in scenes after Flight 72. The second was emotional sound design. We paired her brave flight memories with a cheerful music-box melody. To leave viewers inspired rather than sad, the film then moves to a gentle piano finale. The third was strict ethics and privacy compliance. To protect young participants’ privacy under the competition rules, we recorded no voices or photos of any real children under 18. All voiceovers are 100% synthetic, and all characters are 3D avatars, used with transparent AI disclosures. No official NASA logos were altered.

For research and data, we drew on these sources: NASA/JPL Ingenuity flight logs, the PDS, the MER-B Analyst’s Notebook, the NSSDCA Master Catalog, InSight SEIS data and NASA NIAC aerial vehicle studies. In our visual and animation pipeline, we used Google Gemini for consistent Pixar-style 3D characters, scene generation and storyboarding. We used Fliki AI for animated video production, synthetic character voiceovers and musical sound design. We built the 7-slide pitch presentation with Gamma and PowerPoint. The film is published publicly in HD on YouTube. We did all our work on standard computer and tablet workstations.

Each member of Team Space11 took responsibility for a specific area. Işıknas Gürler, Narrative Lead and Screenwriter, designed the core open-air museum metaphor and built the telescope framing story. She also wrote Ginny’s first-person English script. Kutay Kaan Akdenizli, Aerospace and Telemetry Researcher, studied Ingenuity’s 72 flight logs to make sure the science was accurate (1% atmospheric density, 2,500 RPM). He also analyzed NASA NIAC’s next-generation Mars aircraft concepts. Alp Tuna Gürler, Planetary Science and Exploration Vehicle Archivist, researched Opportunity’s 5,111-sol marathon and its “blueberry” minerals. He also studied Viking 1’s 1976 soil analyses and the more than 1,300 marsquakes InSight recorded.

Işıl Kondakçı, 3D Visual Director and Continuity Editor, wrote the image prompts in Gemini and kept the 3D characters consistent from scene to scene. She also checked that the rotor blades looked right before and after Flight 72. Erva Allahverdi, Synthetic Voice and Sound Designer, managed the synthetic voice characters and narration pacing on Fliki AI. She also handled the emotional audio shift from music box to piano. İsmail Eren, Video Editor, Quality Control Lead and Presentation Architect, put together the final 4:20 cut and confirmed it met the Space Apps ethics and AI rules. He also prepared the YouTube release and structured the 7-slide demo presentation.
